anchor: I celebrate myself, and sing myself
title: The opening and the poem's titles
short: The poem had no title in 1855; it became 'Song of Myself' only in 1881, and the first line itself grew in revision.
body: The 1855 Leaves of Grass printed this as its first, untitled poem, opening simply 'I celebrate myself,'; 'and sing myself' was added later, turning a private boast into an epic invocation (compare 'Arms and the man I sing'), with the poet as both singer and subject. Whitman retitled the poem 'Poem of Walt Whitman, an American' (1856), 'Walt Whitman' (1860), and finally 'Song of Myself' (1881). The second and third lines make the claim democratic at once: whatever the speaker 'assumes' (takes on, and takes for granted), the reader will too, because the very atoms of his body are shared matter. Folsom and Merrill stress this atomic exchange, the circulation of matter among people, animals, plants and soil, as the poem's ground idea. The archive's text, with its 52 numbered sections, is the final (1891-92) version.

anchor: I loafe and invite my soul
title: loafe
short: To idle or lounge; an American word of the 1830s, which Whitman makes the posture of poetic attention.
body: 'Loaf' and 'loafer' were recent American slang of the 1830s (OED), with a disreputable smell of street-corner idleness; Whitman's spelling 'loafe' gives the slang a mock-archaic dignity. Inviting the soul to loaf reverses the Christian hierarchy in which the soul disciplines the body: here body and soul lounge together as equals, a theme developed in the erotic union of section 5. Folsom and Merrill call 'loafe' a marvellous word and read the leaning, idle stance as the precondition of seeing. The 'spear of summer grass' he observes is the book's title-image in miniature: 'Leaves of Grass' plays on the printer's 'leaves' (pages) as well as blades.

title: a spear of summer grass
short: The single blade from which the whole poem grows; grass is the book's master image of the common, the democratic and the perpetually renewed.
body: A 'spear' is a single pointed blade of grass (OED), and the martial word sits oddly and pleasingly beside 'loafe'. Grass grows everywhere and belongs to no one; in section 6 it becomes, in turn, a flag, a handkerchief, a child, a hieroglyph and the hair of graves, and at the poem's close the poet bequeaths himself to the dirt 'to grow from the grass I love'. Against the biblical commonplace that 'all flesh is grass', where grass signifies human transience (Isaiah 40:6-8; 1 Peter 1:24), Whitman makes grass the sign of continuity: what withers returns. Folsom and Merrill read each blade as a token of transfer between the dead and the living.

title: thirty-seven years old
short: Not in the 1855 text: this stanza was added in 1881, moved from 'Starting from Paumanok', where the age had been thirty-six.
body: The stanza beginning 'My tongue, every atom of my blood' is not in the 1855 first edition, whose opening runs straight from the 'spear of summer grass' to 'Houses and rooms are full of perfumes'. Whitman added it in the 1881-82 edition, moving it into 'Song of Myself' from 'Starting from Paumanok' (the 1860 'Proto-Leaf'), where the speaker's age had read thirty-six; in 1881 he changed it to thirty-seven. Whitman, born 31 May 1819, was thirty-six when the first edition appeared in July 1855 and sixty-two when he added the stanza, so the age is a poetic fixing of the poem's moment of first flowering, not a record. By adding it the older Whitman gave the speaker a biography: native soil, three generations of American parents, perfect health. 'Hoping to cease not till death' turns the poem into a life's work, which Leaves of Grass, revised through six editions to 1891-92, literally became. The patriotic genealogy also sits uneasily with the poem's claim to contain multitudes, a tension critics often note.

title: in abeyance
short: Suspended for a while, not abolished: a legal term for a right or title held in suspense, here applied to religious creeds and philosophical schools.
body: 'Abeyance' is originally a law word (Old French abeance, 'expectation'), used of an estate or title waiting for its owner (OED). The speaker does not reject creeds and schools; he sets them aside ('never forgotten') so that Nature may speak 'without check with original energy'. These lines, like the preceding stanza, were added in 1881. The thought is close to Emerson's call in Nature (1836) for 'an original relation to the universe' instead of inherited systems, and Whitman had sent Emerson the 1855 book. The verb 'harbor' (shelter, give port to) makes the speaker a hospitable place where good and bad alike may speak 'at every hazard'.

anchor: Nature without check with original energy
title: Whitman's line
short: Unrhymed, unmetred long lines built on repetition and parallelism, modelled partly on the King James Bible's verse rhythms.
body: Whitman abandoned rhyme and regular metre for the 'free' line, whose unit is the breath and the syntactic clause; the long lines in this edition are broken by indented turnovers, which are printing necessities, not new lines. Coherence comes from parallelism ('I lean and loafe', 'I harbor ... I permit'), anaphora (lines beginning with the same word, as in the 'Or I guess' series of section 6) and the catalogue. Scholars have long linked the method to the parallelism of Hebrew poetry as heard in the KJV Psalms and prophets, and to oratory and opera, which Whitman loved. The line enacts its own claim: like 'Nature without check', it is not trimmed to a pattern.

title: Section 6: the child's question
short: The poem's great meditation begins with a child's unanswerable question and a speaker who admits he does not know.
body: The question has no quotation marks, so the child's words and the speaker's slide into each other. The admission 'I do not know what it is any more than he' is the starting point of the section's method: instead of a definition, a series of guesses, each a metaphor, which together move from the self ('my disposition') to God, to birth, to democracy and finally to death. Folsom and Merrill note that the child brings the grass in 'full hands' as a gift, and that this section is where the poem's thinking about death and recycling life begins in earnest. Whitman divided the poem into 52 numbered sections only in 1867; in 1855 this passage ran on unbroken.

title: 'Or I guess': anaphora and provisional metaphor
short: Each guess is offered tentatively and none cancels the others: meaning is multiplied, not fixed.
body: The repeated opening 'Or I guess' (anaphora) turns the stanza into a catalogue of alternatives, a characteristic Whitman structure. 'Guess' was also ordinary American speech for 'think' or 'suppose', so the solemn subject is approached in a colloquial voice. The first guess, 'the flag of my disposition, out of hopeful green stuff woven', reads the grass as a banner of the speaker's temperament, green being the traditional colour of hope; the third (l. 7) makes the grass 'itself a child, the produced babe of the vegetation', the offspring of the earth as the questioner is the offspring of his parents. The provisional grammar matters: Whitman's metaphors are tried on, not imposed.

title: the handkerchief of the Lord
short: God as a lover who drops a scented, monogrammed handkerchief so that we will pick it up and ask whose it is.
body: The conceit borrows a courtship custom: a lady drops a handkerchief, initialled in the corner, as a hint to a suitor. Nature is a 'remembrancer' (a reminder, a token; the word was also the title of an Exchequer official, OED) dropped 'designedly', on purpose, so that we 'remark, and say Whose?'. Whitman thus restates the argument from design (nature as evidence of a maker, as in Paley's Natural Theology, 1802) as flirtation rather than proof: the gift provokes the question but the name stays 'someway' hidden. Folsom and Merrill gloss the image as God's mystery inviting pursuit.

title: hieroglyphic
short: The grass as a sacred script, the same sign written everywhere, which must be read and translated.
body: Egyptian hieroglyphs had been deciphered by Champollion only in 1822, and Egyptology was fashionable in 1850s New York; Whitman made many visits to Dr Henry Abbott's Egyptian Museum on Broadway while composing Leaves of Grass and praised it in print in 1855. A hieroglyph is a picture that is also a word, and 'uniform' makes this one democratic: the same character in 'broad zones and narrow zones'. The figure prepares the later wish to 'translate the hints' of the dead, and section 52's 'untranslatable'. Scholars debate how far the Egyptian material shaped the image, as against the general Romantic idea of nature as a book of signs.

title: Kanuck, Tuckahoe, Congressman, Cuff
short: Slang types of Americans and neighbours: a French Canadian, a lowland Virginian, a politician and a Black man, all given 'the same'.
body: 'Kanuck' (Canuck) is a French Canadian; 'Tuckahoe', from an Algonquian word for an edible root, was a nickname for planters and people of tidewater Virginia, east of the Blue Ridge, as opposed to the 'Cohees' of the backcountry; 'Cuff' (from the Akan day-name Kofi) was a common, often contemptuous name for an enslaved or Black man. The line yokes the lowly and the powerful in one breath, as the grass grows 'among black folks as among white'. Written in the years of the Fugitive Slave Act (1850) and the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854), the equality is pointed, though readers note that Whitman still uses the period's demeaning labels.

title: the beautiful uncut hair of graves
short: The section turns to death: grass on graves as the hair of the buried, still growing, never cut.
body: The image is at once macabre and tender (the popular belief that hair keeps growing after death lies behind it), and the adjective 'beautiful' insists on the tenderness. From here the guesses become a meditation on the dead: the grass may 'transpire' from the breasts of young men, from old people, from infants taken from their mothers' laps, so that the grass becomes 'the mothers' laps'. Folsom and Merrill single out the phrase as one of the poem's most striking. Many readers have felt that the passage anticipates Whitman's Civil War hospital poems, though it was written six years before the war.

title: transpire
short: To breathe out or exhale through pores, as plants give off moisture; the grass is breathed up out of the dead bodies.
body: The older, literal sense of 'transpire' is to pass off as vapour through the skin or the surface of a leaf (OED), a botanical term Whitman uses exactly: the grass is the dead's breath made visible. The everyday sense, 'to come to light, become known', is also active, since the grass 'tells' the hints that the speaker wishes he could translate. The tentative 'It may be' repeated three times keeps the speaker in the mode of guessing.

title: uttering tongues
short: The blades of grass become tongues: the dead speak through them, and the poet's task is to translate.
body: The leaf-tongue metaphor grows from the previous line's 'roofs of mouths'; the dark grass seems to come up out of the mouths of the dead. 'They do not come from the roofs of mouths for nothing': the grass is not mute, it signifies. The speaker wishes he 'could translate the hints', confessing the limit of his power just as he confessed ignorance in the first line; the circle closes in section 52, where he calls himself 'untranslatable'. Folsom and Merrill read the grass as a coded language of the dead that needs fearless translation.

title: 'there is really no death'
short: The smallest sprout proves that life recycles matter endlessly; death is only a moment of passage.
body: The answer to 'What do you think has become of the young and old men?' is a materialist and mystical one at once: the dead are 'alive and well somewhere' because their substance returns as new growth. 'All goes onward and outward, nothing collapses.' The conviction resembles ancient atomism (Lucretius' cycle in which nothing returns to nothing, De rerum natura 1.215-64) and contemporary chemistry of the conservation of matter, as much as any Christian doctrine of resurrection. Folsom and Merrill call the base materials of life immortal in Whitman's view.

title: 'and luckier'
short: The famous deflation: dying is not only different from what we supposed, but luckier. Serene wisdom or provocation?
body: The colloquial last word, a gambler's or a child's word, refuses the solemn vocabulary of elegy. Some readers take it as Whitman's genuine serenity, the fruit of the section's cycle of matter; others hear deliberate provocation or bravado, a claim the poem asserts rather than demonstrates; still others hear a wry acknowledgement that no one can know, since the section began with 'I do not know'. The line is identical in the 1855 text, so it belongs to the poem's first conception.

title: The spotted hawk
short: The poem's last section: a hawk reproaches the speaker for his chatter and idling, and he answers that he too is wild.
body: The hawk 'accuses' him of 'gab' (idle talk, a colloquial word) and 'loitering', which picks up the 'loafe' of section 1: the bird, purposeful and silent, rebukes the human poet's leisurely song. Instead of defending himself, the speaker identifies with the bird: 'I too am not a bit tamed'. Folsom and Merrill read the hawk's cry as a sign of the speaker's own wildness and his merging with the natural world in the poem's closing movement.

title: untranslatable
short: The self cannot be fully rendered into another language or form, just as the grass's hints could not be translated.
body: The word answers section 6, where the poet wished he could 'translate the hints' of the dead. Now he himself is the untranslatable text. Folsom and Merrill read it as the self's resistance to being carried from one form into another (and, playfully, as a challenge to the poem's many translators). The claim fits the poem's end, in which the speaker dissolves into air and earth and can be found only by searching.

title: barbaric yawp
short: A raucous, uncivilised shout; the poet's anti-genteel voice, sounded over the roofs of the world.
body: 'Yawp' (a variant of 'yelp', from Middle English) means a harsh or hoarse cry, and Whitman's line is its best-known use; 'barbaric' recalls the Greek barbaroi, those whose speech sounded like 'bar-bar' to Greek ears, that is, outsiders to polite language. Whitman claims that outsider status proudly: his poetry is not tamed by European decorum or by rhyme. The 'roofs of the world' echo the 'roofs of mouths' in section 6. The phrase became the poem's most quoted self-description and a motto for American plain speech.

title: scud
short: Low, ragged clouds driven fast by the wind; here the last light clouds of dusk, which seem to wait for him.
body: 'Scud' is a sailor's word for vapoury cloud driven swiftly before the wind (OED). The dusk 'holds back' for the poet and 'flings my likeness' (his shadow) out over the 'shadow'd wilds' as faithfully ('true as any') as the shadows of other things, then 'coaxes' him into vapour. The speaker is about to become weather. Folsom and Merrill treat the scud as one of the last images through which the self scatters into the landscape.

title: effuse ... lacy jags
short: He pours out his flesh like vapour and lets it drift in lace-like, ragged tatters.
body: To 'effuse' is to pour out or shed (OED, from Latin effundere); a 'jag' is a jagged projection or a ragged scrap of cloth or cloud (OED). 'I depart as air' turns death into evaporation, and 'I shake my white locks at the runaway sun' gives the old poet a last defiant gesture at the setting sun. The language of dissolution is cheerful rather than mournful, continuing section 6's claim that death is a passage into other forms.

title: under your boot-soles
short: The poet bequeaths himself to the dirt and becomes the grass, which the reader treads underfoot.
body: 'Bequeath' is the language of a will: the speaker's legacy is his body, given to the soil, to return as the grass of section 6. The 'spear of summer grass' of section 1 thus becomes the poet himself; the humblest, most trodden thing is where he will be found. The 1855 text reads 'bootsoles'. The image completes the poem's cycle of atoms and its democratic stance: he will be under every reader's feet, not on a pedestal.

title: good health ... filter and fibre
short: Though the reader may not understand him, the poet will nourish them like food, purifying and strengthening their blood.
body: The poem ends where it began, with 'perfect health' (section 1) and shared atoms: the poet's matter will 'filter and fibre' the reader's blood, cleansing it like a filter and giving it fibre or strength. Reading becomes a bodily transfusion rather than an act of comprehension; 'You will hardly know who I am or what I mean' frankly admits that the poem resists interpretation. Folsom and Merrill read the close as a handing over of the poet's body to grass and his words to readers.

anchor: I stop somewhere waiting for you
title: The last line
short: An open ending: the poem ends not with arrival but with a promise to wait. In 1855 the line had no full stop.
body: The final stanza's imperatives ('keep encouraged', 'search another') turn the reader into a seeker, and the last line reverses the roles of the whole poem: now the poet waits, and the reader must travel. In the 1855 edition the line read 'I stop some where waiting for you', with no closing punctuation, so that the poem literally did not close; later editions, including this text, add a period. Folsom and Merrill pose the missing stop as a question about how an unfinished ending shapes our response.
